sentences.text:
For Respondent(s) : Mr. J.P. Bhardwaj, Pp.
_____________________________________________________ Hon'Ble The
Chief Justice Order 10/08/2017
1.
On 21.10.1984 a sample of sesames oil was taken by the Food Inspector from the shop of the petitioner at the bus stand.
The sample was opined to be adulterated on account of olice acid being found to be 4.5% as against 3% prescribed by the standard.
The defence of the petitioner, even put to the witnesses of the prosecution was that the petitioner was not selling sesames oil.
He was selling cigarettes and betel leaves (Pan) from the shop.

As per him the Food Inspector used to purchase cigarettes from him on credit and when he demanded money the Food Inspector took the sample from his house where he had kept the sesames oil for domestic consumption.
2. Convicted vide decision dated 14.03.1995 and sentenced to undergo S.I. for a period of six months, the appeal filed has been dismissed on 20.09.1997.
3. Contention of learned counsel for the petitioner is that notwithstanding both Courts noting the defence, have not dealt with the evidence relatable thereto.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioner draws my attention to the testimony of Madan Singh (PW-3)
who during cross-examination admitted that all documentation took place at the house of the petitioner.
The Food Inspector Nemi Chand examined as PW-2 during cross-examination evaded the issue by saying that he was not aware whether the petitioner's shop and residence were at a different places.
5. It is in this context that the contention advanced is that the learned Courts have ignored vital evidence while dealing with the defence.
6. I have perused the impugned decisions.

Except noting the defence taken, there is no discussion on Ashok Kumar vs State on 10 August, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19072098/
1 this aspect of the matter.

sentences.text: 7. The prosecution has led no evidence that the petitioner was in the business of sale of sesames oil.
It is the positive case of the petitioner that he was not.

In this connection the testimony of PW-3 assumes importance during his cross-examination and he admitting that all documents were prepared at the residence of the petitioner.
8.
Truth emerges from small openings.
The testimony of PW-3 leans in favour of the defence taken by the petitioner.
9. There is yet another problem with the impugned judgments.

They overlook the fact that compliance of Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was made on (3 of 3)
[CRLR-435/1997] 19.04.1985.
As noted above the sample was lifted on 21.10.1984.
Being a natural product rich in oxygen sesames oil tends to turn into olice acid.

The proof is that when compliance was made with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the notice was served upon the petitioner, he exercised the right to have second sample to be sent to the Central Laboratory.
Percentage of olice acid was found to be 7%.
Delay in sending the notice to the petitioner has caused prejudice.
This aspect has been overlooked by both Courts below.
10. The petition is allowed.
Impugned judgments are set aside.
The petitioner is acquitted for the offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The sentence imposed as also the fine are set aside.

(PRADEEP NANDRAJOG)CJ.
